beginner.text: Brent crude is the global oil benchmark that most of the world uses to price oil trades. It jumped to over $108 this week before pulling back to around $90 as fears of a prolonged Middle East war eased. Brent prices directly affect what countries pay to import oil, so movements here ripple through energy bills worldwide.

moderate.text: Brent hit $108.20 at the week's high, its highest level since early 2023, as the Hormuz blockade removed roughly 20% of global oil supply from the market. Iraq and Kuwait declared force majeure as storage at land terminals backed up with barrels that could not be exported. Brent retreated to $90 on March 10 following Trump's ceasefire signals and G7 reserve release discussions. The Brent-WTI spread widened slightly, reflecting Brent's greater sensitivity to Gulf supply disruptions.

expert.text: Brent's divergence from WTI during the Hormuz crisis reflects the physically grounded nature of the global benchmark: Brent tracks the seaborne crude market most directly affected by Middle East supply disruption, while WTI is anchored by US domestic production and Cushing storage dynamics. At $90, Brent still reflects a 10 to 12 dollar war premium. The key structural question is whether Iraq and Kuwait can resume normal export volumes once Hormuz reopens, or whether the force majeure period has disrupted maintenance and contract schedules in ways that extend the supply shortfall.

beginner.text: Natural gas prices spiked sharply this week after Qatar, the world's largest LNG exporter, halted shipments following Iranian attacks on Gulf energy infrastructure. Gas is used to heat homes, generate electricity, and power factories, so higher prices feed quickly into household bills and industrial costs.

moderate.text: Henry Hub natural gas hit $4.50/mmBtu, up 40.6% in the past month, driven by two concurrent shocks: the Qatar LNG export halt after Iranian strikes on Gulf infrastructure, and persistent below-average US storage levels heading into spring. European TTF gas jumped even more sharply as the EU scrambled to secure alternative LNG supply. At $4.50, Henry Hub is well above the EIA's pre-war February forecast of $4.30 for full-year 2026.

expert.text: The gas market is absorbing two simultaneous shocks: a physical supply disruption via the Qatar LNG halt and a structural tightening from US production constraints during the winter drawdown. The Strait of Hormuz's role in LNG markets is less direct than in crude, but Qatar's LNG terminal proximity to the conflict zone is creating buyer reluctance to commit to spot cargoes. European buyers, who need to refill storage to 90% capacity by November, face a drastically compressed timeline and are paying any price to secure supply. TTF and JKM Asian LNG markers have surged to three-year highs.

Gold fell briefly to $5,080 on Monday as some investors sold gold to cover losses elsewhere, but it bounced back quickly. At over $5,000, gold has more than doubled in the past three years.

moderate.text: Gold's 1.5% drop to $5,080 on March 9, while oil surged 13 to 18%, was a textbook liquidity event: institutional investors with large profitable gold positions sold to meet equity margin calls. The metal recovered to $5,145 on March 10 as the dollar weakened and safe-haven demand reasserted. Central bank buying, which has been running at record levels for three consecutive years, provides a structural floor. The week's CPI and PCE data are the next catalysts: a soft print would support gold by weakening the dollar; a hot print would complicate the picture.

expert.text: Gold's divergence from the energy inflation narrative on March 9 is analytically important: in a genuine stagflation scenario, gold should eventually rally as real rates fall and the dollar weakens. The Monday selloff was not a signal of changed fundamentals but a mechanical margin-call liquidation. The $5,000 level, which represents approximately 3% of global household net wealth, has become a structural support as central bank and retail allocations have doubled over five years. J.P. Morgan's $5,000 Q4 2026 target now looks conservative; the conflict-driven safe-haven bid could push gold to $5,500 to $5,800 if the Iran war extends beyond Q1.

Silver is both a precious metal that investors buy for safety and an industrial metal used in solar panels and electronics, so it is sensitive to both safe-haven demand and global growth expectations.

moderate.text: Silver fell 3.7% in the past session, underperforming gold, as the industrial demand component of silver pricing reacted negatively to global growth fears triggered by the oil shock. Silver's gold ratio, currently around 59x, suggests silver remains relatively undervalued on a historical basis. J.P. Morgan's 2026 silver forecast of $56/oz was set before the conflict; with the Iran shock pushing gold higher and industrial demand from solar and EV infrastructure remaining structurally robust, silver could significantly outperform that target.

expert.text: Silver's underperformance versus gold during the March 9 risk-off episode reflects the dual-nature pricing dynamic: the industrial component of silver demand priced in growth fears, while the monetary component provided only partial safe-haven offset. Silver's sustained deficit, running for the third consecutive year according to the Silver Institute, means any recovery in industrial sentiment and safe-haven demand convergence could create a powerful simultaneous bid. Citi's pre-conflict bull case of $58/oz by Q4 2026 is plausible; a scenario of extended conflict, dollar weakness, and accelerating solar deployment could push silver toward $100/oz.

beginner.text: Copper is often called the metal with a PhD in economics because its price reflects global growth expectations. Copper slipped slightly this week as the Iran war raised fears of slower economic activity. At over $5 a pound, copper remains historically expensive, reflecting strong long-term demand from electric vehicles and renewable energy infrastructure.

moderate.text: Copper fell 2% to $5.00/lb as global risk-off sentiment and growth concerns outweighed the structural supply deficit narrative. The LME copper all-time high of $13,238/tonne in January 2026 reflected genuine physical tightness: a projected 1 million tonne supply deficit in 2026 driven by AI data centre construction, EV infrastructure, and grid electrification. The Iran shock creates a short-term demand pessimism overlay on an unchanged structural supply story. Copper typically recovers quickly from geopolitical selloffs as the underlying demand fundamentals reassert.

expert.text: Copper's 2% selloff is consistent with its pattern of behaving as a high-beta global growth proxy in the initial phase of geopolitical shocks, before the structural supply deficit reasserts. The 1 million tonne 2026 deficit is driven by demand sources, AI data centres consuming 10x the copper of conventional facilities, EV buildout, and grid expansion, that are entirely disconnected from the traditional commodity demand cycle. Institutional rotation from gold and silver into copper that was underway before the conflict may accelerate once the binary war risk resolves. Citi's $12,000 base case and $14,000 bull case represent 20% and 40% upside respectively from current levels.

beginner.text: Wheat prices rose 5.1% over the past month, driven by cold weather damaging crops in parts of Europe and the United States, and ongoing disruptions to grain shipments from the Black Sea region. Higher wheat prices feed into the cost of bread, pasta, and many other foods, affecting household budgets globally.

moderate.text: Global wheat prices rose 1.8% in February, according to the FAO, following reports of frost and winter kill risk in parts of Europe and the US. Logistics disruptions from Russia and ongoing Black Sea tensions also contributed. The Iran conflict has added a secondary logistics risk: disruptions to shipping routes through the Red Sea and Persian Gulf affect some wheat trade flows, particularly to Middle Eastern and North African import markets that depend on Gulf port access.

expert.text: Wheat's 5.1% monthly move reflects a convergence of supply-side risks that were building before the Iran conflict: frost damage in key winter wheat regions, Russian export logistics constraints, and tight global stocks-to-use ratios near multi-year lows. The FAO Cereal Price Index's February uptick, after five consecutive monthly declines, signals that the deflationary trend in agricultural prices may be reversing. The Iran war adds a demand-side shock for Middle Eastern and North African importing nations, which typically use Gulf ports for wheat deliveries and now face both higher commodity costs and higher shipping costs.

beginner.text: Corn prices rose around 3% this month as the Iran conflict raised concerns about global economic activity and trade routes. Corn is used for animal feed, ethanol fuel, and food products worldwide, making it a broad indicator of agricultural market conditions. Prices remain below their 2022 highs.

moderate.text: Corn prices have held firm at 472 cents per bushel, up 3.1% over the past month, despite broader commodity market volatility. Global corn prices were broadly stable in February according to the FAO, though the Iran conflict introduces upside risk via two channels: reduced US ethanol blending demand if consumers cut driving, and increased feed cost pressure on livestock producers already dealing with tight cattle supplies.

expert.text: Corn's relative stability reflects its more domestically anchored demand structure compared to wheat or soybeans. US corn demand is split roughly equally between ethanol, animal feed, and export, meaning that global shipping disruptions have a more modest direct impact. The agricultural price index is projected to decline modestly in 2026 under the World Bank baseline, but the Iran shock introduces upside risk via energy cost passthrough: nitrogen fertiliser, derived from natural gas, becomes significantly more expensive when gas prices spike 40-plus percent, raising 2026 crop production costs and potentially reducing planted acreage if farmers price in margin compression.

beginner.text: Soybean prices edged up slightly this month. Soybeans are crushed into oil and meal used in food, biofuels, and animal feed, making them one of the world's most important agricultural commodities. Brazil and the United States are the two largest producers, and trade between them and China shapes the global price.

moderate.text: Soybeans at 1,080 cents per bushel, up 1.1% on the month, reflect a calm physical market despite geopolitical noise. Brazil's soybean harvest is progressing well, with the 2025/26 crop expected to set a new record near 170 million tonnes. Mercosur's EU trade agreement, signed in January, is a medium-term positive for Brazilian soybean exporters, reducing tariff barriers to the EU market. The key price driver this week is China demand, which remains the dominant swing factor for global soy trade.

expert.text: Soybean prices are navigating three simultaneous forces: a record Brazilian harvest that is bearish on supply, persistent Chinese demand that is supportive on the demand side, and an Iran-conflict backdrop that creates logistical and demand uncertainty. The World Bank forecasts agricultural prices to edge slightly lower in 2026, with soybeans in particular benefiting from easing trade tensions between the US and China under the October 2025 Busan truce. The Mercosur-EU deal, pending ratification, would provide Brazilian soybeans with tariff-free access to the EU over a phase-in period, shifting some trade flows from US to Brazilian origin over the medium term.

Gold has reached new all-time highs above $5,100 per ounce as investors rush to safe-haven assets amid the Middle East conflict and global market uncertainty, a significant boost for gold-mining countries like South Africa.

Natural gas prices are sharply higher after Iranian drone strikes forced Qatar (the world's largest LNG exporter) to declare force majeure and halt operations, cutting off about 20% of global liquefied natural gas supply.
moderate: WTI Crude at $90.90/barrel (+36% WoW) and Brent at $92.69 (+27%) reflect acute Strait of Hormuz disruption: ~140 million barrels of regional crude is stranded, OPEC+ announced a larger-than-expected production increase but barrels are largely inaccessible given the shipping halt; analysts warn Brent could exceed $100 if the conflict lasts beyond 4 weeks.

Gold at $5,158/oz continues its multi-year bull run, now compounded by the Iran conflict flight-to-safety bid; the metal benefits simultaneously from central bank buying (EM reserve diversification), USD weakness earlier in 2026, and an acute geopolitical risk premium; silver at $84.31 is tracking higher on both safe-haven and industrial demand.

Agricultural commodities are rising as the Middle East conflict disrupts shipping: wheat (+5.8% weekly) faces a dual shock: the Middle East is a large wheat importer and key shipping routes are disrupted; soybeans (+3.2%) are supported by China's continued import demand and Brazilian export strength; corn (+4.3%) reflects biofuel demand as energy prices spike globally.
expert: The WTI/Brent spread has narrowed to ~$1.79 (from a typical $3-5), reflecting the global nature of the supply shock and US SPR release speculation: with approximately 9mb/d off the market from facility damage and precautionary shutdowns, and OPEC+ production geographically constrained by Hormuz closure, the market's clearing mechanism is IEA strategic reserve coordination, a tool that buys weeks, not months, of price suppression.

Gold's rally above $5,100 represents a regime shift in the gold-real-rate relationship: previously gold tracked inversely to US real rates (TIPS yields); the current gold strength despite higher real rates (driven by CPI upside from energy) suggests the safe-haven bid is overriding the rate-discount mechanism, a pattern historically associated with tail-risk scenarios where the monetary policy reaction function itself becomes uncertain.

Agricultural commodity supercycle dynamics are being reinforced by the Iran shock: fertiliser (natural gas-intensive in production) prices are spiking with LNG, creating a second-order agricultural supply shock for the 2026/2027 growing season; the FAO food price index is likely to reverse its recent moderation; and the combination of energy and food price inflation in a single shock is historically the most damaging inflation configuration for EM sovereign credit.

commentary.beginner: Commodities are the raw materials that power the global economy - things like oil, gold, wheat, and copper. Their prices affect everything from the cost of filling your car to the price of bread. When oil rises, transport gets more expensive, which pushes up prices across the board. Gold often rises when people are worried about the economy.
commentary.moderate: Commodity markets are signalling mixed conditions. Energy prices remain subdued on soft China demand and resilient US shale supply, while gold continues to rally on central bank buying and safe-haven demand. Agricultural commodities are pressured by strong Southern Hemisphere harvests. The copper-to-gold ratio - a classic growth proxy - has been declining, consistent with a slowing global cycle.

Gold's move above $2,900 is driven less by real rates (still positive) and more by EM central bank reserve diversification (PBOC, RBI, NBP cumulative buying ~1,100t in 2024-25). Dr. Copper's sideways action reflects offsetting forces: China property drag vs. electrification pull. The GSCI/SPX ratio near 40-year lows signals extreme undervaluation of real assets vs. financial assets.

beginner.label: Oil Swings Wildly as Iran War Dominates Markets
beginner.body: Oil prices hit $119 a barrel on Monday morning before crashing back to around $88 by Tuesday. The swing happened after US President Trump suggested the military campaign against Iran was nearly over and that oil tankers could soon move freely again through the Strait of Hormuz. Prices are still much higher than before the war started, which means fuel costs remain elevated for most households and businesses worldwide.

beginner.label: US Lost 92,000 Jobs in February
beginner.body: The US economy shed 92,000 jobs last month, a shock result that nobody expected. Unemployment climbed to 4.4%. The Federal Reserve now faces a painful choice: cutting interest rates could help the job market, but oil prices are already pushing inflation back up. Doing both at the same time is nearly impossible, which is why financial markets are unusually nervous right now.

beginner.label: Stock Markets Bounce Back on Peace Hopes
beginner.body: After a brutal Monday selloff, stock markets recovered on Tuesday when Trump hinted the Iran conflict could end soon. The S&P 500 gained about 0.8% on Monday's close and Asian markets stabilised on Tuesday. Gold is trading around $5,145 an ounce, holding near record highs as investors stay cautious. The situation remains fragile, and markets will swing sharply on any new developments from the Middle East.
beginner.source: Trading Economics / Reuters / JM Bullion, March 10, 2026

moderate.label: WTI's $38 Intraday Swing: The Biggest Single-Day Oil Move in History
moderate.body: WTI crude touched $119.48 overnight before collapsing to $86 as Trump signalled that the Hormuz blockade was ending and the G7 prepared to release strategic reserves. The 35.6% weekly gain through March 9 was the largest in WTI's recorded history. By March 10, front-month WTI settled near $88, still up roughly 23% year-to-date. The reversal shows how heavily war-premium pricing has dominated physical markets, and how vulnerable that premium is to a single diplomatic headline. February CPI on Wednesday and PCE on Friday will show whether energy passthrough has begun hitting core inflation.

moderate.label: US Payrolls -92K: Stagflation Enters the Base Case
moderate.body: February nonfarm payrolls fell 92,000 against a consensus of +55,000, the first payroll contraction since 2020. Federal employment drove much of the decline, shedding 85,000 jobs tied to DOGE-related cuts. Healthcare added 112,000, masking near-zero private-sector ex-healthcare growth. Unemployment rose to 4.4%, its highest since early 2023. The combination of a contracting labour market and a 23% oil spike is the definition of stagflation, and markets have now pushed Fed cut expectations to September at the earliest. Wednesday's CPI is the next pivot point.

moderate.label: Risk Assets Stabilise: S&P Recovers 0.8%, Gold at $5,145
moderate.body: Wall Street executed a partial reversal on Monday as Trump's comments about a swift end to military operations triggered a collapse in crude from $119 to $86, removing the immediate stagflation worst-case. The S&P 500 closed up 0.83%, the Nasdaq gained 1.38%, and the VIX retreated from 30 toward the mid-20s. Gold pulled back slightly to $5,145 on a firmer dollar before recovering. European shares bounced on Tuesday. Markets are pricing a binary outcome: a quick peace deal sends oil back toward $70 and equities higher; a protracted conflict risks embedding energy inflation and forcing the Fed's hand.
moderate.source: Trading Economics / Reuters / JM Bullion, March 9-10, 2026

expert.label: Hormuz War Premium Collapses on Trump Comment: The $90 Liquidity Void Is Now the Map
expert.body: WTI's intraday range of $98 to $119.48 on March 9, followed by a collapse to $86 on Trump's ceasefire comment, is a textbook demonstration of how binary geopolitical optionality reprices in an illiquid physical market. Saudi Arabia's forced output cuts and Iraq's 70% production decline at its three main fields created a genuine scarcity signal, but the Trump comment triggered the exact flash crash J.P. Morgan identified as the risk: a $20 move into the $90 liquidity void in minutes. Front-month WTI at $88 on March 10 still prices meaningful conflict duration, roughly 10-12 dollars of war premium above the pre-war $75 baseline. Every week of Hormuz disruption adds approximately 0.25pp to global CPI. The duration of that premium, not its existence, is the macro variable that will define the FOMC's path through Q2.

expert.label: US February Payrolls -92K: Dual-Mandate Conflict Reaches Critical Mass
expert.body: The K-shaped deterioration in the US labour market sharpened in February: healthcare added 112,000, masking federal government shedding 85,000 (DOGE-linked), IT contracting 18,000 (AI displacement), and near-zero private-sector ex-healthcare growth. Unemployment at 4.4% now sits above the FOMC's December median forecast. The FOMC meeting on March 17-18 is the first real test of the committee's reaction function under simultaneous supply-shock inflation and labour-market weakness. Easing signals risk embedding energy-inflation expectations above 3.5%; tightening signals risk accelerating labour-market deterioration. The Fed's only plausible communication strategy is to acknowledge the dilemma explicitly and remain data-dependent, buying time until the February CPI print clarifies whether oil passthrough is accelerating into core.

expert.label: Risk Asset Anatomy: Monday's Reversal Was Rational, Tuesday's Stability Is Fragile
expert.body: Monday's reversal in US equities, S&P 500 up 0.83%, Dow up 0.5%, Nasdaq up 1.38%, was mechanically driven by crude's collapse from $119 to $86, which removed the immediate worst-case stagflation premium from equity discount rates. Gold's recovery to $5,145 on March 10 after Monday's liquidity-driven selloff to $5,080 confirms the safe-haven bid remains structurally intact beneath the tactical noise. The VIX term structure, front-month near 30 with the 3-month at 24, still prices binary resolution. Tuesday stability is conditional on no new military escalation from Iran's IRGC, which has demonstrated willingness to extend operations into UAE territory. The February CPI release on Wednesday is now the dominant macro catalyst for the week, with a soft print potentially compressing the stagflation narrative and giving the FOMC room to signal patience without implying a hawkish pivot.
